I have Existential Gardening Questions
Ok. 

So I bought a house in a 6b (Niagara) zone, previous owners were Italians who loved their garden, owned this place for 45 years. 

I am not Italian, I am actually from a Russian family. Yet, I feel obliged to continue this 84-square-meter-soil-flat-bed-of-full-sun legacy. 

(And donate to the food bank) 

My entire backyard is soil, and I happen to hate grass. So I’d like to keep it this way. 

There’s some garlic popping out from their work last year. Thank you previous owners. 

There are some other green plants I do not understand that have survived. 

Yet. 

I’ve grown tomatoes and peppers. That’s it. Maybe a bean. One bean. And once my goldenberry bush made a berry and then it died because of my poor choices. 

I’d like to create raised zones of garden with mulch paths between the squares or rectangles to reduce the span a little bit. 

I’ve started a few seedlings as well. I’ve got 10 Zucchini plants that seem to tolerate my incompetence. Like 12 tomato plants, but I’m not pushing my luck, it’s probably gonna be like 6. 

I accidentally bought lettuce seed tape. What the fuck. I didn’t mean to do that. But now I have lettuce seed tape.

Radishes, an indeterminate amount of seedlings have also survived mostly with new leaves. 

I know I need more to cover this farm. I’ve sprouted other types of seedlings, but I think they’re  already in need of palliative care. 

Where I live, it seems like the frost risk is fairly low right now. 

With the span of garden I have, what the heck do I do? What tools do I need? I have hands, a shovel, and a hand rake. 

Oh and there are buried fig trees. 

I am in over my head, I’m well aware. 

But let me try to swim. 

What else can I sprout right now? Should I direct sow? What tools do I need?

Edit: I want to say that EVERYTHING you guys are saying so far is super helpful and easing my nerves surrounding this.

The mystery around how to fertilize and water watermelons!
I live in the North of Italy with a good South exposure. I've been growing tomatoes, bell peppers and cucumbers with great success for the past 4 summers. This year I have 3 watermelons and 2 pumpkins seedlings I want to grow as well so I was reading about what different care they need – I also want to learn better about the micronutrient needs of all my plants. I'm really confused as I've been reading dozens of sources both in English and in Italian and the information is drastically different.

To sum it up, I read these 2 opposite information about watermelon:  
1) Don't fertilize in the first month from transplant, especially avoid Nitrogen before flowers appear, because this could cause blossom abortion – I can't find the source anymore, but it was a pdf from a plant production and technology university, it seemed probably the most reliable source I found. Then add some nutrients, especially Calcium after flowers appear, then Potassium in the last 15-30 days when the fruit grows.  
2) Add Nitrogen after transplant so the plant grows well, as you do with most plants, then general micronutrients. All sources seem to agree about Potassium in the late stage.

I'm so confused about should I add or avoid Nitrogen before the flowers? And if the first advice is true, is it also true for other plants like night shades?

Also regarding watering I read you should water watermelons/pumpkins 2-3 times a week (which is what I'd naturally do in summer in my weather since it tends to be really hot from June to August), but on some other blogs I found the suggestion to only water watermelons once every week-10 days, checking the moisture a couple inches under soil level and only watering when it's dry, and to stop watering them a couple weeks before picking the fruit, so that the sugars concentrate and the texture and sweetness increase.

Again, what should I do? I don't want to obsess over these things, I've successfully grown tomatoes and peppers without putting too much thought in it so far, but now reading these opposite advices I feel I want to understand what should I do especially with water and Nitrogen since I would have given plenty of water and Nitrogen to all of my plants had I not read different advice.

​

Thank you in advance!

Newbie Braised Short Rib Fail (help please)
The short version: I made braised short ribs in a Staub Dutch oven tonight and clearly made a bunch of mistakes. This is the first time trying something like this. I followed what appeared to be a really simple recipe on YouTube (enter “Williams Sonoma Braised Short Ribs).


Longer version: I really like cooking, but am not skilled or that great a cook. I really want to get better at this thing. 

I’m a dad of 4 boys and do the bulk of cooking in our house. I’m not very good but I do enjoy it.  I do know my way around the grill (I make a lot of grilled chicken, various steaks, pork chops and tenderloin). My boys don’t complain much but I want to up my game a bit.  I recently made some really solid “one pot pastas” (I kinda impressed myself to be honest and that rarely happens). 

Feeling inspired, I researched a bunch of “one pot recipes” and found my way to some Dutch Oven recipes. 

I bought a Staub Dutch oven and decided to try my hand at short ribs. I never made anything like this before.  I watched a bunch of YouTube videos and settled on the aforementioned recipe. I was confident. 

I bought quality bone in short ribs from a local butcher.

In hindsight, the recipes didn’t have measurements. So I estimated based on what the guy was doing. 

I started with some olive oil, browned the short ribs “fat side down” and took them out and set aside.  Turned the heat down a bit to medium.

Next I went in with the onions for a few mins. Then carrots for a few mins. Then garlic until fragrant.  Then tomato paste and let that brown a bit.

(Again, newbie here). I felt like there was maybe a little too much oil/fat at this point (compared to what I saw in videos). 

Here’s where I think I started to go wrong. I added flour and maybe a tad more than I should have (just under 1 cup). 

It clumped up so much. But I let it cook like the video said knowing I still had to add the wine and beef broth. 

So I did. Added some wine and stirred. Then added some beef broth. Stirred.

Then added back my browned short ribs. They were probably half submerged. Lid went on and in the oven at 350. 

At 1.5 hours I checked it.  Meat was 195. And the liquid was simmering. 

I know it has to be “fork tender” and mine wasn’t. And the liquid seemed thick, so I added some more beef broth, lowered the oven to 325, back in it went. 

I cooked it for about 4hrs total and pulled it.  Honestly I think it could have been left in longer. 

The meat was still fatty but I think leaving it in longer would solve that. What was cooked was actually pretty decent!

Where I think I went wrong, The “sauce” was very thick and brown (like a gravy). And very fatty. I feel like most that I have seen are a darker “burgundy” color. Mine looked like thanksgiving day gravy. Why?  Should it be this way?

I tried to explain exactly what I did. I’d appreciate any feedback. I really want to try to figure this out!

(Looks like I can’t post photos here. But I have a few)

I really appreciate any tips!  My failures are 100% my own and I’m eager to learn.

Fried Cheesy Fishstick Springrolls
My kids don't like fishsticks much so I was looking for a way to make it better for them. I ended up finding a recipe for shrimp tacos. 

I took the recipe for the sauce. The OG recipe calls for a lot of fresh ingredients, but I substituted for powders and such and then added some stuff for a preferred flavor. Sour cream, mayonnaise (I used Kewpie bc I like it best), lime juice, rice vinegar, green Tabasco (instead of jalapeños, garlic, onion, paprika, chili powder, cayenne powder, olive oil (instead of vegetable oil), cumin, salt and pepper. It also calls for cilantro but I skipped that.

I oven baked some frozen fish sticks while making the sauce. When they were done, I wet a spring roll wrap and added shredded cheese, 2 fishsticks, and drizzled some of the sauce. I rolled it up and pan seared it on each side and repeat until I had as many as I needed. I also tried a couple with only fishsticks and mac and cheese. 

Only one kid liked the ones w sauce and neither liked the mac and cheese ones. I thought it was all good tho. Sorry for the lack of measurements, I just threw the ingredients together and tasted it then adjusted. Also, sorry I didn't get any pics before eating.

Things That Help Me Help You As An Employee
Edit- These are things that will probably help you get your food faster or with less errors and heartache. You’re adults use your power of discernment. 

1)If it’s not on the menu then we aren’t trained to do it. People will ask for Nachos, Quesoritos, because it’s on the “secret menu”, I just have to say no and offer you a manager. 

Quesadillas, at least in my store, are online only. If you want one without any sides get a “three pointer” which is just the meat and cheese in a burrito. 

2) Ask for your side tortilla at the beginning. Don’t order it at the end cause then you’re gonna be waiting. 

3) Never say what you don’t want on your food. If you say “no tomatoes” and it’s busy you have infinitely increased the chance of getting tomatoes on your food. 

4) Wait to say what you want on the side until the end (or as they give the food to the next employee) because if not you infinitely increased the chance of it getting in your food. 

4.5) *If* you’re going to ignore that then instead of “black bean on the side” say “a side of black beans”. 

5) I’m not a fish, most of the time we have space in the memory and will remember more than one item. If I ask you for the next thing, just tell me rather than waiting for me to put rice before you tell me what beans you want. 

6) Pro tip, don’t let the thing on the top of your bowl be any of the spicy sauces, Queso, sour cream or guac because it will get stuck on the lid, always end with lettuce or cheese. It also makes it easier for me to close a burrito without getting stuff on my gloves. 

7) Ask the cashier for prices because we often don’t memorize them and that’s your best bet. 

7.5) Read the signs, above and below, they’ll tell you stuff that you might want to know like the prices, if the Apple Pay machine is broken or if a food is out of stock 

8) Should have put this earlier, just ask for “extra” at the beginning of anything except for meat, guac, or Queso, chances are they won’t charge you extra for it so you won’t have to worry. 

9). We are on camera, often have a manager within earshot, and have even been written up for giving to much food, plus all the other people who cook the food blame me for giving it out, with all this in mind I’m not trying to be “stingy”. 

10) Sides usually take more time and some stores charge if you get 3 or more. If you’re trying to microwave it just don’t add the lettuce, keep the veggies (tomatoes, corn), guac, or sour on the side. Most hacks are bullshit it’s just more work for us and often no extra food for you. 

11) If you want more food, bowl, always. 

12) If we don’t have it on the line mentally assume if it’s not there. Ask, sure, but don’t expect it to appear. If there’s something you won’t eat your bowl without check if it’s there. Don’t wait for food more than 2 minutes there are other good cheap local restaurants (probably).

13) If you can pay with card (or Apple Pay) do that. There’s a National change shortage and I don’t want you to be upset about 23¢. The price will not swing in your favor, that $12.08 chicken bowl is now $13

14) We cannot take tips if we have gloves on so wait till it’s not busy. You’ll give a tip for the burrito girl and the cashier will pocket it since managers can’t help because we’re not even allowed tips (in my store). 

That’s all I got.

 **Type:** Salad

**Keywords:** Bulgarian shopska salad step by step, Bulgarian cuisine, Bulgarian salads, Bulgarian recipes, Bulgarian shopska salad recipe

**Recipe Yield:** 4

**Preparation Time:** 20 minutes

**Total Time:** 20 minutes  


**Recipe Ingredients:**

* 2 large tomatoes
* half green bell pepper
* half a large Dutch cucumber
* 1 head of red onion
* 100 grams of fresh Bulgarian white cheese (can be feta)
* Salt
* extra virgin olive oil or normal oil
* vinegar (optional)
* black olives
* parsley

**Recipe Instructions:** We wash all the vegetables well and as you can see in the photos on the next page we cut them all. First dice the tomatoes and put them in a bowl. Cut the cucumber into slices cut in half and add it to the tomatoes. Cut the pepper into small strips and add it to the bowl. Cut the onion into small strips as in the photo and add it to the rest of the cut vegetables. Cut the parsley, add to the bowl, salt, pour olive oil and mix.

Grate the white cheese directly into the bowl that already contains the vegetables. Add the olives and serve like this. We can mix directly before putting in smaller dishes. We can serve as a salad with the second course. In the recipe I did not mention the amount of oil, salt, vinegar or olives to add, because we add these products to our liking. 

As a curiosity I would like to add that in Bulgaria, many times this and many salads are served before the main course or dinner with a glass of rakia. The bug battle of July 2024. Earwigs, pill bugs, ants, squash bugs, and more
First year gardening, what an onslaught. The biggest surprise is up until now I haven't had any real pest issues outside of pill bugs eating bean stalks. But boy howdy, they all came together this week to fight. This summer has been consistently in the 90F's and even 100F's some days.

Earwigs. What do they love? Moist conditions with daytime cover. What do all my plants need to survive this summer? Moist soil with mulch. Some say they're beneficial, but not in these quantities. They've done a number on my strawberries, and assassinated my pumpkin and sunflower sprouts. I spread DE (diatomaceous earth) and that seems to dissuade them. The oil and soy sauce traps get some, but when I come out at night with a flashlight I see so much more on the foliage. The traps barely put a dent in the population, probably due to the ants.

Ants. They love the soy sauce traps. If there's any solace in the traps, its that so many ants gather around that it scares away most earwigs. I put the trap as close to my new pumpkin seedlings, but the ants start using dirt and twigs to build a bridge into the dish. It's doing my head in. If the ants are always active around the traps, then the earwigs won't go for them. But if the traps are in the right area, there should be enough ants to dissuade earwigs from entering the area. Wrong, 2nd round of pumpkin sprouts had a party of 6 dining, and they didn't even tip me when they left.

Squash bugs. I thought these were just potato bugs or stink bugs looking for a place to chill. Boy was I wrong. Well, too late too wrong. The combination of high heat and squash bugs doing work on the stem of my zucchini killed the water flow. Last week it was pumping out 650G whoppers. Now the whole plant is in the compost bin. I've inspected the remaining leaves on all my summer squash, winter squash, and cucumber plants. I've picked any squash bug I found and dropped them in the bucket. I've squished their eggs and rolled them into the same soapy bucket. I must have overlooked the bugs because everyone frets about squash vine borer so much, I honestly thought "squash bug" was just another nickname.

Player 4 has entered the lobby. I found a curious looking wasp/moth that looked odd. Black body all over, orange band on abdomen, must be a squash vine borer. Great. A little bit more googling showed the single orange band means its just a peach vine borer. (SVB have orange all over abdomen). So my cucurbits are safe, but my new peach trees aren't. I thought Peach pests subsided after springtime! I sprayed neem oil earlier, but thought I was safe now.

I jump over to my peach trees and inspect like a madman. The end of one twig looked off. Not as black or dramatic as examples online. But I pruned it off and slowly cut the sections away revealing a hollow twig with a small grub inside. I sprayed neem oil on both trees again. Hopefully I don't see anymore leafy ends dying off.

Pill bugs. Earlier reddit posts on the subject are a gaslighting campaign against victims of rolly polly abuse. "They only eat dead material". It's like saying humans only use fallen trees for lumber. Almost all my first beans succumbed to them. I removed mulch in the spring since it wasn't as necessary, but they still did damage. They don't care about DE, its snow to them. Neem oil? More like olive oil, they love that on their beanstalk salad. I guess I'm just going to need to grow more mature seedlings next year.

The only plants that haven't had issues are marigolds, tomatoes, sweet potatoes, and basil. Maybe I bit off more than I can chew, but I'm glad I finally got to start a garden this year. Maybe this post will help someone else dealing with these same pests.

I messaged Chipotle on Instagram, and this morning saw they got back to me. They credited me a second kids meal and a free side of guacamole!

  
I couldn't be happier with their response. I very rarely ever "complain" about things because I expect to be shut down or denied. But I'm glad I took the initiative as they went above and beyond in helping us out.

How many people track the cost of recipes to make? I'm horrified at what some of my regular cooking costs, but it's healthy and I can afford it. Is trying to stay frugal making me cheap?
I had some celery, carrots, peppers, and cucumber to use up so bought some groceries to make a marinated vegetable salad to leave in the fridge.  I have only been tracking expenses for the last year and a bit and groceries have skyrocketed in that time, but I am shocked at what I spend to eat as we normally would.

Tomatoes -7 mushrooms-4 broccoli-4 cauliflower-4 cannned mini corn-3 red onion-2 

So $24 plus the dressing-5, cucumber-1, peppers-2, carrots-2, celery-2 that I had in the fridge is $36 to make a large bowl of salad.  It is big and will last a week so it's probably only $2/serving, but I'm finding it mentally wearing to think about how much stuff costs to make.  

It's making me not want to cook and a bit resentful at my husbands family eating at my house all the time, I start thinking oh there are 3 extra people eating 3 different dishes at $2/serving so $18 extra in food and cooking time today. To the point I've been leaving the fridge fairly empty when I'm working for the week since I can cook at work, or portioning out the extra and freezing it when it's something that freezes well.  I don't have to worry about money as I have more than enough and it really is just people eating my leftovers that we would have eaten, so I'm not sure if thinking like this is cheap or frugal?

My friend was telling another girl how cheap I was the other day, I had ordered some parts and was going to change my brakes and rotors myself since the price the dealship wanted was crazy compared to doing it yourself.  So this got me thinking that maybe I am cheap and not just frugal like I thought.
